name: Nova Scotia
summary_text: Nova Scotia stands under the national framework of Canada. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly in Nova Scotia.  Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Most provinces allow the gender marker on official documents to be changed by declaring one's identified gender; Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act removed the prior surgery requirement and replaced it with a declaration supported by a doctor's letter. Federally, identity documents can carry an X marker. Entry into Canada carries no trans-specific friction.  Correctional placement is the weakest point in the Nova Scotia record. The Chronicle Herald reported on 18 March 2025 that a federal judge gave a transgender woman from the Halifax region more time to file her application for judicial review of the decision to hold her in a men's prison while she serves a two-year robbery sentence. The judge cited a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making, and systemic barriers that restricted the applicant's access to her lawyer. Federal policy after Bill C-16 is that transgender prisoners are to be placed according to their gender identity, so the case turns on whether that policy is being applied in the province's custodial system.  Nova Scotia's provincial government operates an explicit inclusion framework rather than restrictive trans-specific legislation. On 8 January 2026 it released the province's first 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan, developed under the Dismantling Racism and Hate Act passed in 2022, described as the first Canadian law of its kind to explicitly acknowledge 2SLGBTQIA+ people, and informed by more than 600 community members through surveys, virtual meetings and consultations. On 10 June 2026 the province announced more than $176,000 through the first round of its 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Impact Grant program.  National hate-crime data does not resolve trans-specific risk in the province. Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents were recorded nationally in 2024, 1% above 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, down 2% in 2024 and up 142% since 2018, with eight provinces recording stable or declining rates. The release carries no Nova Scotia-specific rate or incident count, and it breaks out sexual orientation as a motivation category rather than gender identity, so trans-specific hate-crime volume is not established by this dataset.

name: Nunavut
summary_text: Canada is among the safer large destinations for trans visitors, and Nunavut stands under that national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Federal identity documents can carry an X marker, entry carries no trans-specific friction, and no jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.  Nunavut layers its own statutory protection on top of that federal floor. In March 2017 Nunavut MLAs voted unanimously on third and final reading of Bill 31, amending the territory's Human Rights Act to add gender identity and gender expression alongside sexual orientation as protected grounds. Justice Minister Keith Peterson said the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited. At that point nine provinces and one territory listed gender identity or expression in their human-rights laws, which made Nunavut the first Canadian territory to do so.  Nunavut's Vital Statistics Act now carries a third sex designation on birth certificates. On 18 September 2025 MLAs voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore the non-binary option after the standing committee had struck it from Health Minister John Main's May 2025 bill; the bill then passed third reading. Sponsor Adam Arreak Lightstone said the Government of Nunavut now joins the rest of Canada in recognizing non-binary and transgender individuals.  The territorial government also funds transition-related care. From March 2022 Nunavut's Health Department funded breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty for transgender and non-binary residents under a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal. The local LGBTQ group Positive Space called the step overdue while flagging information gaps for residents outside the capital.  National hate-crime data sets the surrounding risk picture. Statistics Canada's release 'Police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024', published 30 March 2026, records 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents, up 1% over the year and 169% since 2018, a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents motivated by gender identity or expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive annual increase and 184% above 2020. Sexual-orientation-motivated incidents fell 26% to 658, though June 2024 alone recorded 113 incidents against a monthly average near 50. Rates run roughly 2.5 times higher in metropolitan areas than in smaller towns, a gap that matters for a territory with no metropolitan reporting hub.  Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report works through police-reported data including gender identity and expression motivations and supplies national 2SLGBTQ+ victimisation context rather than territorial figures.
